success_patterns: Compare near-identical choices by their full quantifiers and qualifiers, including existence versus uniqueness, generic versus universal claims, and almost-everywhere versus every-value conclusions.
Track the scope of witnesses and constants: a single object or uniform estimate across parameters and times is stronger than parameter-dependent choices or bounds allowed to depend on time.
For almost-everywhere claims, preserve both the underlying measure and the domain on which it is applied, especially when the domain is a restricted or ambient-null subset.

When a choice asserts an exact classification or a sharp quantitative statement, check both inclusion and exclusion claims and do not upgrade a bound to equality or asymptotic equivalence without support.

patch.reasoning: The successful answers depend on resolving small but decisive differences in quantifier scope, dependence, measure, and exactness. Making these checks explicit helps distinguish choices that otherwise differ by only one qualifier or one part of a classification.

edits.content:
## Scope and classification checks
- Keep “generic,” “for every,” and “for almost every” distinct. For an almost-everywhere claim, preserve the underlying measure and the domain of that measure; a measure supported on a restricted locus need not be ambient Lebesgue measure.
- Track the scope of witnesses and constants: one fixed object working for every parameter is stronger than a parameter-dependent family, and bounds uniform over all times or parameters are stronger than bounds whose constants may depend on them. Do not strengthen the stated dependencies.
- Read “exactly one solution” as asserting both existence and uniqueness; “at most one” asserts uniqueness only and may allow no solution.
- For choices claiming an exact list or partition, verify both sides: every included case must satisfy the claim, and every excluded case must meet the stated failure condition. Establishing only the positive cases does not prove the classification.
